ai.title: Alloimmunisation in Transfusion Medicine
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Alloimmunisation is the immune response to foreign blood antigens, most often after transfusion or pregnancy. It can cause delayed haemolytic reactions and complicate future transfusions.

b: Key antigens: ABO, Rh (D, C, c, E, e), Kell, Duffy, Kidd, MNS
Most common alloantibodies: anti‑D, anti‑K, anti‑E, anti‑C
Incidence in low‑resource settings: 5–10% of transfused patients
sections.p: When a patient receives blood from a donor with antigens absent in the recipient, the immune system may produce antibodies. These antibodies can destroy transfused red cells and, if present, cause delayed haemolysis.

t.b: Detects unexpected antibodies before transfusion; a positive screen means cross‑match is required.
Shows if antibodies are coating transfused cells; a positive DAT indicates immune haemolysis.
Elevated reticulocytes suggest haemolysis; a low count may indicate bone marrow suppression.

b: Clinical spectrum: asymptomatic antibodies, delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction (DHTR), hyperhemolysis syndrome
sections.p: Alloantibody formation depends on antigen exposure, immune status, and antigen immunogenicity. In malaria‑endemic areas, repeated transfusions increase alloimmunisation risk.

b: Pregnancy: anti‑D can cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN)
sections.p: Alloimmunisation limits compatible blood availability and can precipitate severe haemolysis. Early detection and antigen matching are vital in resource‑constrained settings.

b: In hyperhemolysis, consider exchange transfusion and high‑dose steroids
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to recognise alloimmunisation, interpret tests, and manage complications. Focus on the sequence of investigations and the rationale for antigen matching.

b: Ignoring the possibility of anti‑K or anti‑E antibodies in patients with normal ABO/Rh typing
sections.p: Students often overlook the need for extended antigen matching in high‑risk groups and misinterpret a negative DAT as no alloimmunisation.

b: Educate patients about the importance of reporting previous transfusions and pregnancies
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care, and prevent further alloimmunisation by matching antigens beyond ABO/Rh.

b: Malaria relapse: parasitemia on smear distinguishes it
sections.p: Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction can mimic acute hemolysis, sepsis, or malaria relapse.

b: Low reticulocyte count in aplastic anaemia
sections.p: Low reticulocyte count may mask haemolysis in bone marrow suppression; a negative DAT does not exclude alloimmunisation if antibodies are low titre.
Urgent care needed if patient develops sudden drop in Hb, severe jaundice, or signs of shock.
